# The Paper {.divider}

## Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning 
- Title: "Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning", Gu et al., 2020, *Review of Financial Studies*

Authors:

Bryan Kelly

::: {.ov-desc}
AQR Capital Management, NBER, and Yale University
:::
:::

::: {.keypoint}
Research question: Can machine learning methods improve forecasting of asset returns?
:::

## Empirical Asset Pricing

- Asset pricing asks why some assets earn higher expected returns than others, and why expected returns change over time
- The risk premium is the expected return in excess of the risk-free rate, the compensation for bearing risk
- It is unobserved. We observe the realized returns, which are dominated by unforecastable news
- Measuring the risk premium is therefore a forecasting problem, e.g., forecast the excess returns of next month using information available today

::: {.keypoint}
Many correlated predictors and an unknown functional form make this a natural application for machine learning
:::

::: {.notes}
Functional form is the mathematical shape of the relation between the predictors and the expected return.
:::

## Forecasting Target (Sec. 1)
- The authors aim to forecast the excess returns of an asset
- Construct an "additive prediction-error model",

$$r_{i,t+1} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_t[r_{i,t+1}]}_{g^\ast(z_{i,t})} + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}$$

- $r_{i,t+1}$ is the excess return (over the T-bill rate) of stock $i$ at time $t+1$
- $g^\ast(\cdot)$ is the forecasting function, the conditional expected return (the risk premium)
- $z_{i,t}$ is the information set (predictors) for stock $i$ at time $t$
- $\varepsilon_{i,t+1}$ is the error term

::: {.notes}
The T-bill rate proxies the risk-free rate. $g^\ast(\cdot)$ is the unknown true conditional expectation (on $z$ our information set) and $g(z;\theta)$ is our attempt to approximate it with a chosen functional form. 
::: 

::: {.notes}
An additive-error model says the outcome splits into two parts that are simply added: a part the information set can predict, and a part it cannot.

Conditioning on the information set, in terms of the conditional expected return.
:::

## Predictors (Sec. 2.1)

:::: {.triad}
::: {.triad-card}
[Stock characteristics]{.tc-tag}

94 characteristics $c_{i,t}$ from the cross-section literature
:::
::: {.triad-card}
[Macro variables]{.tc-tag}

8 variables $x_t$ from Goyal and Welch (2008): dp, ep, bm, ntis, tbl, tms, dfy, svar
:::
::: {.triad-card}
[Industry]{.tc-tag}

74 dummy variables, one per two-digit SIC industry code
:::
::::

Stock characteristics are made to interact with the macro variables,

$$z_{i,t} = (1, x_t^\intercal)^\intercal \otimes c_{i,t}, \qquad p = 94\times(8+1)+74 = 920$$

Here $p$ is the number of predictors

::: {.notes}
The symbol $\otimes$ multiplies each entry of the first list by the whole second list and stacks the results into one longer list, e.g. $(1, x) \otimes (c_1,c_2) = (c_1, c_2, x\cdot c_1, x\cdot c_2)$, and $(2, 3) \otimes (5, 7) = (2 \cdot 5, 2 \cdot 7, 3 \cdot 5, 3 \cdot 7) = (10, 14, 15, 21)$. In the slide, the leading 1 keeps each characteristic on its own while x pairs it with the macro variable, giving 94 × (8 + 1) = 846 terms before adding the 74 industry dummies to reach p = 920.
:::

::: {.small .faint}
dp: dividend-price ratio, ep: earnings-price ratio, bm: book-to-market ratio, ntis: net equity expansion, tbl: Treasury-bill rate, tms: term spread, dfy: default spread, svar: stock variance
:::

::: {.notes}
Stock characteristics are firm-level variables observed for each stock and month, such as size, book-to-market and momentum. They are closely related to anomalies but not the same thing. An anomaly is a documented pattern in average returns that standard asset pricing models do not explain. Many of the characteristics were first documented as anomalies, and the paper builds them "based on the cross-section of stock returns literature". The characteristic is the variable and the anomaly is the return pattern it is linked to, so they are NOT anomalies per se. 
:::

::: {.notes}
SIC code: standard industrial classification, four digit code, a firm's main line of business. The first two digits give the broad industry. For example, 28 is chemicals. 
:::

# Methodology of Paper {.divider}

## Sample Splitting (Sec. 2.1) {.compact}

:::: {.splitbar}
::: {.sb-train style="flex: 18"}
Training: 1957--1974
:::
::: {.sb-val style="flex: 12"}
Validation: 1975--1986
:::
::: {.sb-test style="flex: 0 0 auto"}
Testing: 1987
:::
::: {.sb-rest style="flex: 29"}
Later refits: 1988--2016
:::
::::

:::: {.splitbar}
::: {.sb-train style="flex: 19"}
Training: 1957--1975
:::
::: {.sb-val style="flex: 12"}
Validation: 1976--1987
:::
::: {.sb-test style="flex: 0 0 auto"}
Testing: 1988
:::
::: {.sb-rest style="flex: 28"}
Later refits: 1989--2016
:::
::::

$$ \vdots $$

:::: {.splitbar}
::: {.sb-train style="flex: 47"}
Training: 1957--2003
:::
::: {.sb-val style="flex: 12"}
Validation: 2004--2015
:::
::: {.sb-test style="flex: 0 0 auto"}
Testing: 2016
:::
::::

- The training sample is an expanding window, one more year at every refit
- The validation sample is a rolling window of fixed length, 12 years
- The models are refit once a year, due to computational overhead and low frequency of signal (data/predictor) arrival: 30 estimations instead of 360 over 30 test years
- Each fitted model is tested on the next year only

## Hyperparameters and Validation (Sec. 1.1)

The regularization approaches of the paper rely on hyperparameters, e.g.,

- The penalty parameter (elastic net) 
- The number of components (PLS, PCR)
- The tree depth (random forests, boosted trees)

They control model complexity, and there is little theoretical guidance on how to set them

:::: {.flow}
::: {.fn-navy}
Training
[model on the training sample for given hyperparameters]{.fn-sub}
:::
::: {.fn}
Validation
[evaluate on the validation sample, compute the loss]{.fn-sub}
:::
::: {.fn-amber}
Model Selection
[select hyperparameters with the best validation loss]{.fn-sub}
:::
::::

## Bias, Variance, and Regularization (Sec. 1.3)

:::: {.compare}
::: {.compare-col}
[Flexible models]{.cmp-title}

- A flexible model (nonlinearities, interactions, deep trees, neural networks) can approximate a wide range of functions, so bias is low
- But if it is **too** flexible for the data, it has many parameters to estimate from limited information, so the estimates have high variance and are unstable
- It then fits noise (adapts to the current sample) rather than signal and performs poorly out of sample
:::
::: {.compare-col .cmp-alt}
[Regularized models]{.cmp-title}

- Accept some bias in return for lower variance
- By means of penalties (LASSO, ridge, elastic net), fewer dimensions (PCR and PLS), shallow trees, early stopping, or averaging over trees or seeds
- The degree of regularization is a hyperparameter and can be determined via validation
:::
::::

## Evaluation: Out-of-Sample $R^2$ (Sec. 1.8)

Forecasts are evaluated on the test sample (out-of-sample), pooling all stocks and months,

$$R^2_{\text{oos}} = 1 - \frac{\sum (r_{i,t+1} - \hat{r}_{i,t+1})^2}{\sum r_{i,t+1}^2}$$

- Compares the squared forecast errors of the model with those of a forecast of zero
- A positive $R^2_{\text{oos}}$ means that the model beats a zero-excess-returns forecast (difficult!)

::: {.keypoint}
The benchmark must be motivated and specified by the researcher
:::

::: {.notes}
$$R^2_{\text{oos}} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t+1}} (r_{i,t+1} - \hat{r}_{i,t+1})^2}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t+1}} r_{i,t+1}^2}$$
:::

## The Models

:::: {.steplist style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
::: {.step-row}
::: {.step-title}
OLS+H

:::

:::

::: {.step-row}

:::
::: {.step-desc}
Principal Components Regression on $K$ principal components, the main directions of variation in the predictors
:::
:::
::: {.step-row}
::: {.step-title}

:::
::: {.step-desc}
Partial Least Squares Regression on $K$ components built to covary with the returns (target), not just with the predictors
:::
:::
::: {.step-row}

GLM+H
:::
::: {.step-desc}
Generalized Linear Model: Linear regression on piecewise-polynomial (spline) transformations of each predictor, no interactions
:::
:::
::: {.step-row}
::: {.step-title}
Trees
:::
::: {.step-desc}
Tree-based models: Random forests average many deep trees, boosted trees (+H) sequentially add many shallow trees
:::
:::
::: {.step-row}
::: {.step-title}
Neural networks
:::

Feed-forward neural networks, NN1 to NN5 models have one to five hidden layers
:::

::::

::: {.keypoint}
+H marks models estimated with the Huber loss: squared error for small forecast errors and absolute error for large ones
:::

## Forecast Accuracy in the Paper (Sec. 2.2)

Monthly out-of-sample $R^2$ (percent) -- **Gu et al., 2020 Table 1**

::: {.act-table style="font-size: 0.68em;"}
| Model | All | Top 1,000 | Bottom 1,000 |
|:---------------------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
| OLS+H, all 920 predictors | −3.46 | −11.28 | −1.30 |
| OLS-3+H | 0.16 | 0.31 | 0.17 |
| Elastic net+H | 0.11 | 0.25 | 0.20 |
| PCR | 0.26 | 0.06 | 0.34 |
| PLS | 0.27 | −0.14 | 0.42 |
| GLM+H | 0.19 | 0.14 | 0.30 |
| Random forest | 0.33 | 0.63 | 0.35 |
| Boosted trees+H | 0.34 | 0.52 | 0.32 |
| NN3 (best) | 0.40 | 0.70 | 0.45 |
:::

::: {.small .faint}
+H: Huber loss. Top and Bottom 1,000: the largest and smallest stocks by market value each month. 

NN1 to NN5 range from 0.33 to 0.40 (All), 0.49 to 0.70 (Top) and 0.38 to 0.47 (Bottom)
:::

# Replication {.divider}

## Replicating Gu et al. (2020)

Replication is ultimately unsuccessful, as the paper omits key details. We are not aware of any successful, publicly available replication. 

::: {.act-table style="font-size: 0.72em;"}
| Step | Task | Hurdle |
|:-----|:-----------|:-------|
| 1 Data | Stock returns from CRSP and accounting data from Compustat, both through WRDS | Proprietary data + 1:1 matching |
| 2 Pre-processing | Build 94 characteristics, rank them to $[-1,1]$, lag them, fill in missing values, interact them with the macro variables and add industry dummies | Many choices are not fully stated, post-hoc updates |
| 3 Estimation | Thirteen models with tuning grids, refit once a year over 30 test years | Computing time and memory |
| 4 Evaluation | $R^2_{\text{OOS}}$ | Mismatch of results |
:::

::: {.keypoint}
The raw return data is proprietary (WRDS licence), so I cannot distribute the data
:::

::: {.notes}
You can access the data via the Wharton Research Data Services https://wrds-www.wharton.upenn.edu, where you must create a student account. It took about two days to obtain approval for my account when I created mine, approximately two years ago.
:::

## The Replication Package

::: {.keypoint}
Journals increasingly require authors to publish their **replication code** in full with the paper
:::

The authors have published code for the Monte Carlo simulations in Internet Appendix A, but not for the empirical study.

- Everything that the paper and the Internet Appendix do not state has to be decided by us
- Each such choice can affect the results (next slides)

## Approaching the Data Set

We verify that our data match the description in the paper, asking: Do the discrepancies stem from the data?

:::: {.compare .cmp-sm}
::: {.compare-col}
[Coverage]{.cmp-title}

- 29,925 distinct stocks in our file and "almost 30,000" in the paper 
- Stocks per month are 5,225 in our file and "exceeding 6,200" in the paper 
- CRSP's monthly file itself gives about 5,590
:::
::: {.compare-col .cmp-alt}
[Returns]{.cmp-title}

- 3,742,884 stock-months appear in both our file and CRSP
- 99.93% of these match CRSP's return to within 0.0001 (correlation 0.9992)
:::
::::

## Lacking Information

::: {.overview}
::: {.ov-row}
::: {.ov-label}
Solver for OLS + Huber
:::
::: {.ov-desc}
OLS with Huber loss has no analytical solution and must be minimized numerically. The paper does not state the algorithm applied
:::
:::
::: {.ov-row}
::: {.ov-label}
Scaling of the predictors
:::
::: {.ov-desc}
Not specified. Z-score standardization is the natural default, yet this cannot be assumed

Example: We observe that PLS for Top 1,000 is −0.62% under Z-score std. and −0.30% unscaled, against −0.14% in Gu et al., 2020
:::
:::
::: {.ov-row}
::: {.ov-label}
Grid of hyperparameters
:::
::: {.ov-desc}
Table A.5 lists $K$ as the hyperparameter for PCR and PLS but gives no grid. We searched $K = 1\text{ to } 100$
:::
:::
:::

## Our Replication vs. Table 1

Monthly $R^2_{\text{oos}}$ (percent): All / Top 1,000 / Bottom 1,000. Full panel, test years 1987--2016

::: {.act-table style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
| Model | This replication | Paper, Table 1 |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------:|:----------------------------:|
| OLS-3 | 0.20 / 0.23 / 0.19 | 0.16 / 0.31 / 0.17 |
| OLS | −141.38 / −491.65 / −52.20 | −3.46 / −11.28 / −1.30 |
| OLS, stopped early (calibrated)$^\ast$ | −3.46 / −13.28 / −0.95 | −3.46 / −11.28 / −1.30 |
| Elastic net+H | 0.17 / 0.16 / 0.25 | 0.11 / 0.25 / 0.20 |
| PCR | 0.29 / 0.06 / 0.37 | 0.26 / 0.06 / 0.34 |
| PLS | 0.18 / −0.62 / 0.40 | 0.27 / −0.14 / 0.42 |
| GLM, trees, neural networks | … | … |
:::

::: {.small .faint}
$^\ast$ Gradient descent stopped at a tolerance chosen to match −3.46 for \*All\*. 
Calibration, not replication. Top and Bottom still differ. PCR and PLS use z-score standardized predictors
:::

::: {.keypoint}
GLM, trees and neural networks were not run: given the issues so far and the HPC requirement, there is little reason to do so
:::

## What We Can and Cannot Reproduce

:::: {.dodont}
::: {.do-col}
<h3>Same order of magnitude</h3>
- OLS-3: 0.20% vs. 0.16%
- PCR: 0.29% vs. 0.26%
- Elastic net: 0.17% vs. 0.11%
- The pattern: OLS-3 and the regularized linear models are positive, the full OLS is not
:::
::: {.dont-col}
<h3>Does not reproduce</h3>
- OLS: −141.38% vs. −3.46%
- PLS: 0.18% vs. 0.27% (All) and −0.62% vs. −0.14% (Top 1,000)
- Stocks per month: 5,225 vs. more than 6,200
:::
::::

::: {.keypoint}
Overall, the replication can be considered unsuccessful, that is:

The results of the paper are **not reproducible with the information given**
:::

## Up to you

::: {.keypoint}
You are the referee. The paper reports −3.46% $R^2_{\text{OOS}}$ for OLS and we get −141.38%. 

Which three questions might you ask the authors, and which one matters most?
:::

::: {.notes}
Example replies:
1) Choice of scaling, treatment of outliers and missing values. 
2) Specifics of the OLS + Huber implementation: which algorithm, which convergence settings, and which threshold?
3) Details of data extraction and pre-processing, preferably with associated code. 
4) Can you share your exact replication code?
5) Do you see any explanations for why it appears no one has managed to replicate your results, keeping in mind the notoriety of your paper?
:::

# Explaining Why {.divider}

## Why Does OLS Do Worse Than the Other Models?

Two sources of forecast error: **bias** (the model systematically misses part of the true relation) and **variance** (the estimates are unstable across samples),

:::: {.triad}
::: {.triad-card}
[OLS]{.tc-tag}

[920 coefficients]{.tc-title}

Low bias, but high variance: with noisy returns the coefficients are poorly determined, so the forecasts are unstable too. Paper: $R^2_{\text{oos}} = -3.46\%$
:::
::: {.triad-card}
[OLS-3]{.tc-tag}

[3 coefficients]{.tc-title}

Low variance, but the other 917 predictors are ignored, so the bias is higher. Paper: $R^2_{\text{oos}} = 0.16\%$
:::
::: {.triad-card}
[Regularized models]{.tc-tag}

[Shrinkage or compression]{.tc-title}

Use the predictors, but shrink the coefficients or compress them into a few components: a little bias for much lower variance. Paper: $R^2_{\text{oos}} = 0.11\%$ to $0.27\%$
:::
::::

## Why Does Our OLS Differ From the Paper's?

Our OLS gives $-141.38\%$, the paper's $-3.46\%$. Three differences between our implementation and theirs could explain this,

::: {.act-table style="font-size: 0.68em;"}
| Difference | Possible mechanism | Status |
|:------------------|:-----------------------------|:-----------------|
| Solver for the Huber loss (start, step size, stopping rule) | Stopping early shrinks the coefficients | Matches *All* once calibrated |
| Predictor construction (scaling, missing values) | Changes which columns are extreme or near-constant (potential source of instability) | Not tested |
| Data | Different sample of stocks: 5,225 vs. more than 6,200 per month | Not tested |
:::

::: {.keypoint}
We matched the paper's number by calibrating the solver, but a match does not prove the cause
:::

# Wrapping Up {.divider}

## What the Replication Shows

:::: {.triad}
::: {.triad-card}
[The picture holds]{.tc-tag}

Full OLS fails, while OLS-3 and the regularized models do well
:::
::: {.triad-card}
[The numbers do not]{.tc-tag}

Our numerical results differ from those of the paper, the OLS results in particular
:::
::: {.triad-card}
[Unstated choices matter]{.tc-tag}

Choices left open, such as the solver and the scaling, change the results a lot
:::
::::

::: {.keypoint}
In your own work, document every implementation choice and report how sensitive the results are to it
:::

# Appendix {.divider}

## Early Stopping/Termination Is Regularization

Our OLS by accelerated gradient descent from zero (monthly $R^2_{\text{oos}}$, percent)

::: {.act-table style="font-size: 0.66em;"}
| Tolerance | Iterations (median) | All | Top 1,000 | Bottom 1,000 |
|:----------|:-------------------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| 1e-5 | 369 | −12.86 | −50.09 | −5.29 |
| 3e-5 | 187 | −8.06 | −32.72 | −3.12 |
| 1e-4 | 107 | −4.95 | −19.06 | −1.56 |
| 2e-4 | 78 | −3.46 | −13.28 | −0.95 |
| 5e-4 | 51 | −1.92 | −8.04 | −0.32 |
| 1e-3 | 36 | −1.03 | −5.32 | 0.07 |
| 1e-2 | 11 | 0.07 | −1.82 | 0.49 |
:::

::: {.small .faint}
Fewer iterations shrink the coefficients toward zero, as early stopping does for networks (Sec. 1.7). This moves OLS to the paper's order of magnitude but nothing suggests this is the method of choice. We fail to select a tolerance to replicate both All, Top, and Bottom of the paper
:::

## Theory: The Variance of the OLS Estimator

$$y = X\beta + \varepsilon, \qquad \hat\beta = (X^\intercal X)^{-1}X^\intercal y, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta \mid X) = \sigma^2 (X^\intercal X)^{-1}$$

where the errors $\varepsilon$ have variance $\sigma^2$

- If a column of $X$ is almost all zeros, or almost a copy of other columns, the data say very little about its coefficient
- The variance of that coefficient estimate is then very large

::: {.keypoint}
Little variation in a predictor and high correlation between predictors have the same effect: the coefficients are poorly determined
:::

## Theory: What Regularization Does

Ridge regression penalizes the size of the coefficients,

$$\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}} =(X^\intercal X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\intercal y$$

- All coefficients are shrunk towards zero with a strength governed by $\lambda$ ($\lambda = 0$ $\to$ OLS)
- Adding $\lambda I$ to $X^\intercal X$ makes the estimates less sensitive to the data, which lowers the variance at the cost of bias
- Early stopping has a similar effect: gradient descent starts with all coefficients at zero and moves towards the OLS solution, so stopping early leaves them closer to zero
<!-- - Early stopping has a similar effect: gradient descent starts at zero, and stopping early leaves the coefficients closer to zero than OLS -->

## Demo: Data

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.standard_normal((1200, 110))  # 10 relevant and 100 useless predictors
y = X[:, :10] @ np.full(10, 0.3) + rng.standard_normal(1200)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.8, 
                                                    shuffle=False)
```

## Demo: OLS

```{pyodide}
ols_10 = LinearRegression()
ols_110 = LinearRegression()

ols_10.fit(X_train[:, :10], y_train)
ols_110.fit(X_train, y_train)

r2_ols_10 = 1 - np.sum((y_test - ols_10.predict(X_test[:, :10])) ** 2) / np.sum(y_test ** 2)
r2_ols_110 = 1 - np.sum((y_test - ols_110.predict(X_test)) ** 2) / np.sum(y_test ** 2)
```

## Demo: Ridge

```{pyodide}
ridge_10 = RidgeCV(alphas=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000])
ridge_110 = RidgeCV(alphas=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000])

ridge_10.fit(X_train[:, :10], y_train)
ridge_110.fit(X_train, y_train)

r2_ridge_10 = 1 - np.sum((y_test - ridge_10.predict(X_test[:, :10])) ** 2) / np.sum(y_test ** 2)
r2_ridge_110 = 1 - np.sum((y_test - ridge_110.predict(X_test)) ** 2) / np.sum(y_test ** 2)
```

## Demo: Results

```{pyodide}
print("OLS R2_OOS, 10 predictors:    %.2f" % r2_ols_10)
print("OLS R2_OOS, 110 predictors:   %.2f" % r2_ols_110)
print("Ridge R2_OOS, 10 predictors:  %.2f" % r2_ridge_10)
print("Ridge R2_OOS, 110 predictors: %.2f" % r2_ridge_110)
```

::: {.keypoint}
Ridge matches OLS with 10 predictors and rescues it with 110
:::
